articles.title: Washington cities spend millions on Flock cameras. Do they solve crime?
articles.content: Washington cities have invested at least $2 million in Flock ALPR cameras, with contested results. Police report benefits: Everett shows a 67.81% drop in stolen vehicles versus prior three-year averages; Spokane County credits Flock with 88 vehicle recoveries and 150 arrests; Yakima cites 688 supported investigations including homicides. However, vandalism and privacy concerns prompted eight Washington cities to cancel or suspend cameras. National controversy followed revelations that federal agencies accessed data for immigration and abortion-related investigations. Washington's new Driver Privacy Act restricts data use near schools and reproductive clinics and bans immigration-enforcement applications. Early cancellation can create financial liability.
articles.author: The Center Square

articles.title: Flock cameras: How a police tool sparked a surveillance revolt in the US
articles.content: Flock Safety operates a subscription model with over 120,000 cameras across 49 states. Each camera captures 6-12 snapshots per vehicle, recording license plates, vehicle models, visible damage, and timestamps using AI. Data retention was reduced from 30 days to 7 days in August 2026. Law enforcement can share information through a nationwide network, which advocates say incentivizes broad sharing (share nationally to gain access to others' data). Flock reports its cameras assisted over 1 million investigations in 2025 and helped locate nearly 10,000 missing people. Critics argue indiscriminate collection enables tracking of movements, workplaces, healthcare, and protests. Documented misuse includes a Kentucky officer who allegedly tracked an ex-girlfriend over 2,000 times and a Revere, MA officer who tracked a former girlfriend. Florida DOT suspended permits; Texas Gov. Abbott froze funding; Tempe, AZ ended its contract; Congress launched investigations.
articles.author: Victoria Hoffmann

articles.title: Lynchburg ends Flock contract, but camera debate isn't over
articles.content: Lynchburg City Council voted 6-1 on September 3 to terminate its Flock contract, ending use of license plate-reading cameras and gunshot-detection devices. Councilman Chris Faraldi's resolution calls for keeping cameras offline until the agreement expires in April to avoid additional payments, while Councilman Marty Misjuns plans an alternative requiring removal by October. Faraldi warned expedited removal could trigger a $35,000 termination fee. The police department had already paused Flock operations weeks before the vote, and debate over timing and cost continues.
articles.author: Charley Vicario

articles.title: Flock cameras trigger nationwide backlash over privacy concerns, police abuse
articles.content: More than 50 cities and counties have canceled or deactivated Flock cameras in 2026. Florida's state transportation office revoked local law enforcement's ability to place license plate readers on state highways; Texas Gov. Greg Abbott paused state funding; Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro indicated support for a bipartisan bill banning the devices statewide; and Sen. Josh Hawley announced a formal investigation, requesting internal documents. Misuse examples include a Kentucky officer arrested for allegedly tracking an ex-girlfriend over 2,000 times and six Savannah, Georgia police employees fired in August for suspected abuse; the Institute for Justice documented over 100 ALPR abuse incidents. Flock cameras have been vandalized in at least 36 states, including devices sawed down and shot.
articles.author: Max Zahn

articles.title: DeFlock started from one man's curiosity. Now Flock cameras are a midterm issue
articles.content: Software engineer Will Freeman created DeFlock after noticing Flock ALPRs during a 2024 cross-country drive, building a website mapping camera locations. The project grew into a national movement after media attention (notably Tucker Carlson's coverage increased traffic sixfold), becoming an organizational hub helping communities challenge Flock. Though Freeman's team is small (5-10 people), opposition has become a midterm campaign issue, with figures like Texas candidate Gina Hinojosa and Ohio Republican Vivek Ramaswamy criticizing the network and Sen. Hawley citing police misuse. Flock announced changes including tightening retention to seven days, which Freeman argues remain insufficient.
articles.author: Claire Carter

articles.title: Bipartisan push for investigation into Flock Safety cameras grows amid misuse allegations
articles.content: Lawmakers from both parties are scrutinizing Flock's nationwide ALPR network. Republican Sen. Josh Hawley opened a congressional inquiry, citing 120,000 cameras across 49 states conducting over 20 billion monthly scans and arguing Congress never authorized this infrastructure. Progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders announced plans for legislation prohibiting Flock and mass surveillance technology. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called the cameras 'out of control,' and Tempe, Arizona discontinued the service after documented misuse. Flock emphasizes crime-solving benefits including locating missing persons and trafficking suspects. The controversy reflects growing bipartisan tension between public safety and privacy.
articles.author: Joe St. George

articles.title: Hawley launches investigation into AI-powered Flock Cameras as privacy concerns arise
articles.content: Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, opened an investigation into Flock's AI-powered camera network. He argues the company created an unprecedented national surveillance infrastructure with over 120,000 cameras across 49 states scanning more than 20 billion vehicles monthly, and that the vast majority of Americans captured have committed no wrongdoing. He criticized pooling data into a searchable national database rather than supporting discrete local investigations, and demanded CEO Garrett Langley provide documentation on data-access safeguards by September 8, 2026, invoking Supreme Court recognition that comprehensive movement records differ from ordinary public observation.
articles.author: Gabe Swartz

articles.title: Scoop: Senate Republican investigates Flock cameras
articles.content: Sen. Josh Hawley, chair of the Senate Judiciary subcommittee on crime and counterterrorism, is investigating Flock Safety's network of 120,000 AI-powered cameras used to track vehicle movements. His letter demands documents on data collection, retention, law enforcement access policies, and known misuse incidents since 2021, plus information on camera accuracy, security protocols, and revenue sources. The probe responds to bipartisan concerns about privacy safeguards, documented police misuse, and false-positive arrests. Flock said it welcomes the opportunity to provide information and emphasizes crime-solving and missing-persons benefits. Hawley indicated potential subpoena authority if voluntary compliance fails.
articles.author: Andrew Solender

articles.title: Lansing City Council adopts resolution to end Flock camera contracts
articles.content: Lansing City Council adopted a resolution to terminate all contracts with Flock Safety, directing the mayor and police department to end existing agreements. Residents packed chambers opposing the technology, with some saying they adjusted routes to avoid the cameras. Police defended the system: Chief Rob Backus emphasized help locating missing persons and investigating human trafficking and theft. First Ward Councilmember Ryan Kost, who proposed termination, cited civil liberties concerns, calling the devices 'little trail cams taking pictures 24/7' that operate reactively after crimes rather than preventing them.
articles.author: Sarah Poulos

articles.title: A cautionary perspective on Flock cameras (Guest Commentary)
articles.author: Karl Bickel

articles.title: City of Santa Barbara to End Contract with Flock Cameras
articles.content: Santa Barbara is ending its Flock contract amid concerns about data sharing with federal immigration enforcement, declining to renew when the agreement expired August 23. Staff recommended replacing twelve Flock devices with Verkada cameras on a closed, city-owned network accessible only to authorized police, whose database cannot be shared with outside agencies or multi-jurisdictional networks. Police Chief Kelly Gordon emphasized the department would keep exclusive control over configurations, permissions, retention, alerts, and administration. The city evaluated Axon and Motorola but found Verkada offered superior privacy protections and cost-effectiveness.
articles.author: Ryan P. Cruz

articles.title: Another Oregon city ending its Flock cameras contract, despite reporting some success
articles.content: Winston, Oregon ended its contract with Flock, becoming Douglas County's first municipality to do so. The police department operated eight roadside cameras at $24,000 annually. Chief Brandon Sarti acknowledged the technology helped solve crimes, including a homicide, but budget cuts exceeding $215,000 made discontinuing it a 'clear choice.' Sarti cited public concerns about surveillance and potential immigration access, though he said federal agencies had no access to their system. Nearby jurisdictions (Josephine County Sheriff, Talent City Council) also ended or suspended programs. Oregon recently restricted ALPR data retention to 30 days unless investigation-related.
articles.author: Justin Higginbottom (Jefferson Public Radio)

articles.title: Asheville mayor calls for city to cancel Flock Safety contract
articles.content: Asheville Mayor Esther Manheimer announced she will call for a vote to terminate the city's Flock contract at the August 25 council meeting, following resident concerns about 24-hour surveillance. She explained a moratorium would be insufficient because the contract does not permit removal without termination. She said, 'I have heard clearly from Asheville residents, and I'm calling on Asheville to turn off the Flock cameras,' and called for transparent policies governing data already collected. She acknowledged termination won't resolve all privacy concerns but emphasized working with the community on protective policies.
articles.author: Lorenza Medley

articles.title: 'Get the Flock Out': Western Massachusetts residents push back against automated license plate readers
articles.content: A growing Massachusetts and national movement opposes Flock ALPRs. Agawam City Councilor Christine Rickmon questioned police use and faced pressure to apologize. Police defend the cameras as investigative tools, but critics warn they enable mass tracking without warrants or suspicion, storing movement data via AI. Concerns include documented police misuse and data sharing with federal immigration agents. At least ten western Massachusetts departments deployed Flock this year. Activists organized through DeFlock and the Muslim Justice League are mapping cameras and advocating removal; some municipalities (e.g., Easthampton) ended contracts after residents investigated spending. Advocates argue the technology disproportionately affects marginalized communities.
articles.author: divina cordeiro; Dusty Christensen

articles.title: How Flock cameras help lead ICE to illegal immigrants
articles.content: The article reports that ICE uses Flock's license plate camera technology to track and identify undocumented immigrant drivers. It notes cooperation between ICE and more than 2,300 agencies nationwide, some involving Flock data sharing, enabling ICE to monitor vehicle movements via ALPRs. The piece frames this as a mechanism supporting deportation operations, notes the Trump administration is evaluating the program, and mentions some Nevada legislators proposed protective policies on plate-reader data. (Captured via summary; full text paywalled.)
articles.author: Anna Giaritelli

articles.title: Despite 'New' Updates, Flock's Creepy Cameras Remain a Major Civil Liberties Threat
articles.content: The ACLU argues that more than 120,000 Flock ALPRs nationwide photograph every passing vehicle and log detailed information into a massive centralized database. Flock claims 'local control,' letting departments decide what offenses other customers can search their data for. Default retention recently dropped from one month to one week, with an 'Evidence Mode' allowing longer holds tied to cases. The ACLU emphasizes the systems enable tracking of vehicles and applying AI to uncover occupants' private 'patterns of life,' and contends recent company updates do not fix the core problem: the system still collects and shares the movements of millions of people not suspected of any crime.
articles.author: Chad Marlow

articles.title: Flock Updates Privacy, Accountability, Security, and Transparency Safeguards
articles.content: Flock announced safeguards: a new 7-day default retention (down from 30 days) with an 'Evidence Mode' to preserve data for active/cold cases; mandatory 'Audit Assistance' (by end of 2026) that flags abnormal activity plus a proactive lockout; required case codes for all searches (by end of 2026) with emergency searches flagged; offense filtering so communities can restrict which offense types other agencies may search (e.g., allow stolen-vehicle but block immigration queries); mandatory multi-factor authentication; an independent security review by Bishop Fox (findings due September 2026); and a coordinated vulnerability disclosure program. The company says 1,500+ agencies have published Transparency Portals and that customers own their captured data.

articles.title: Flock cameras and license plate readers are everywhere. Can we trust cops with them?
articles.content: Lindsey Isaacs spent seven months in legal turmoil after Florida Highway Patrol arrested her based on a Flock camera identification wrongly connecting her Dodge Durango to a fatal hit-and-run that killed three. Despite available evidence (damage inconsistencies, mismatched paint transfer), investigators relied on the plate reader without proper verification. While Flock claims 96% character accuracy, some real-world audits show far higher failure rates. The article also documents intentional abuse, with officers using Flock to stalk ex-partners. The technology captures over 20 billion vehicle reads monthly across 49 states, raising privacy concerns despite crime-solving claims.
articles.author: Joe Lancaster

articles.title: Flock cameras explained: How automated plate readers work and their impact in South Texas
articles.content: Flock Safety produces ALPRs mounted along roadways that photograph license plates and log where and when a vehicle was seen, capturing details like make, model, and color. Agencies use them to locate vehicles connected to stolen cars, missing persons, and violent crimes. The Bexar County Sheriff's Office operates 35 cameras that read more than 700,000 plates in 30 days. Systems are part of networked surveillance infrastructure tracked by groups like DeFlock.org. Controversy centers on privacy, oversight, and data retention. Officials in Georgia and North Carolina were caught misusing the cameras; Guadalupe County terminated its contract citing vandalism and public scrutiny.
articles.author: Zaria Oates; Emilio Sanchez

articles.title: Roseville Police Find Flock Cameras Misread 71% of License Plate Alerts, Raising Surveillance Concerns
articles.content: A Roseville Police Department analysis determined that Flock's system incorrectly read license plates in 71% of stolen-vehicle and felony alerts. Between 2023 and 2024, Flock sent 1,427 such alerts; police review found the misread rate applied to exactly those alerts most likely to trigger a law-enforcement response. Flock disputed the findings, stating that under optimal conditions its cameras accurately read more than 96% of plate characters, and attributed Roseville's problems to non-standard deployment (rear-only positioning for privacy, older hardware positioned higher and farther than recommended). Roseville police confirmed officers must independently verify alerts before enforcement and reported no documented wrongful stops, while noting 2025-2026 accuracy data was incomplete.
articles.author: Pranathi Srinivasa

articles.title: Map Shows Cities That Have Rejected, Deactivated Flock Cameras
articles.content: Numerous U.S. cities are rejecting Flock ALPR cameras over privacy and surveillance concerns. Per DeFlock, 95 cities have rejected ALPR systems while over 122,000 cameras exist nationwide. Actions vary: El Cerrito, California deactivated cameras after declining renewal; Appleton, Wisconsin and Bloomington, Indiana canceled contracts after public opposition; Shoreline, Washington rejected proposals before installation. DeFlock reports 22 jurisdictions deactivated cameras, 47 canceled contracts, and 25 rejected proposals. Concerns center on data storage, federal access, and movement tracking, while supporters argue Flock aids investigations and vehicle recovery.
articles.author: Amanda Greenwood

articles.title: Inside the growing police use and misuse of Flock's license-plate reader cameras
How an Automatic License Plate Recognition System Works
articles.content: Flock's vendor explainer describes the ALPR workflow: cameras capture vehicle images; software reads the plate plus supported vehicle details (make, color, body type, distinguishing characteristics); the system adds time and location so detections can be searched, mapped, or connected to incidents; customer-configured hot lists generate alerts for vehicles of interest (stolen vehicles, AMBER Alerts, warrants); and detections become searchable records deleted automatically after 7 days by default unless a different retention is set. Flock claims over 98% plate capture, over 96% OCR accuracy, and over 97% plate-state accuracy, and states an ALPR read should be treated as an investigative lead requiring human review, not a standalone basis for enforcement.

articles.title: Police say Flock cameras help solve crimes, but critics call them an invasion of privacy
articles.content: Over 100,000 AI-powered license plate reader cameras operated mainly by Flock scan billions of vehicles monthly without driver awareness. Supporters cite crime-solving benefits, with Flock claiming the technology helps resolve 800,000 to one million crimes annually, including locating a stolen vehicle with an abducted infant. Critics raise privacy concerns: Denver resident Chrisanna Elser was wrongly accused of theft based on camera footage matching her vehicle; a YouTuber accessed dozens of Flock feeds across cities, exposing security vulnerabilities. Opponents worry about warrantless nationwide searches and immigration enforcement uses. Several cities canceled contracts amid backlash; the company signals openness to regulatory frameworks.
articles.author: Paul Solman; Mary Fecteau

articles.title: What are Flock cameras, and why are they controversial in Berkeley?
Dozens of Innocent Motorists Have Been Pulled Over, Detained at Gunpoint, or Jailed Due to AI License Plate Camera Errors
articles.content: The Institute for Justice documented at least 27 confirmed cases of innocent motorists wrongfully stopped, detained, or arrested due to ALPR errors since 2018, with most after 2023; about two-thirds involved officers drawing guns. Examples: a Sherwood, Arkansas couple detained at gunpoint (Feb 2026) with a six-week-old in the car after a misread; a San Diego arrest (Nov 2025) based on 'vehicle signature' technology matching the wrong car, with one passenger jailed nearly a month; and Morristown, Tennessee grandparents detained at gunpoint (June 2024) after an 'O' was misread as '0.' Roughly one-third of errors were machine-based (obstructions, character confusion); about two-thirds were human errors. Flock claims 93% accuracy, which critics note still yields enormous absolute error given 20+ billion monthly reads.
articles.author: Christopher Ingraham

articles.title: Flock Cameras Are Tracking More Than License Plates: Here's Where All That Data Goes
articles.content: Beyond plate numbers, Flock's AI creates detailed 'vehicle fingerprints' cataloging make, body type, color, damage, and features such as aftermarket wheels and roof racks. Cameras also capture drivers and pedestrians via 'people detection' software, allowing searches using descriptions like 'man in blue shirt and cowboy hat.' Flock's 'Raven' system detects critical sounds (gunshots, drag races, fireworks, accidents) and records three-second audio clips. The Drone as First Responder program deploys AI-enabled drones to investigate 911 calls and ALPR alerts. The article contrasts this with traditional plate reading, describing a shift from reactive identification toward proactive, multi-dimensional tracking aggregated into searchable databases shared across law enforcement networks.
articles.author: Alec Hively

articles.title: Deflock, an open-source project mapping license plate readers
How Effective Is Flock? 2025 Impact Census Results
articles.content: Flock released its 2025 Impact Census, surveying nearly 700 law enforcement agencies across 43 states. Reported findings: about one in five cleared cases involved Flock assistance; the technology supported roughly 1 million criminal investigations nationwide; over 10,000 missing persons were located annually (about 27 daily); and 42% of customer agencies reported Flock helped recover at least half of stolen vehicles in their jurisdictions. Flock describes a two-phase methodology anchoring survey responses to FBI crime data, claiming the largest study of police ALPR usage and outcomes ever conducted. (Vendor-reported figures.)

articles.title: ICE Taps into School Security Cameras to Aid Trump's Immigration Crackdown
articles.content: An investigation found police departments using school district security cameras, including Flock ALPRs installed at Texas school districts, to support federal immigration enforcement. Audit logs from six Texas districts show out-of-state officers conduct far more queries than school personnel. Over one month, Alvin Independent School District's eight cameras were searched more than 733,000 times by 3,100 agencies, including 620 immigration-related searches by 30 agencies across multiple states. School officials appeared unaware their data supported immigration enforcement. Researchers and educators worry campus-safety surveillance is being repurposed without guardrails or transparency.
articles.author: Mark Keierleber

articles.title: Does Flock Share Data With ICE? Here's Flock's Answer
articles.content: Flock states it does not work with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and has no ICE contract. It emphasizes customers own and control all data, with sharing decisions made by the data-owning agency, not Flock; ICE cannot directly access Flock cameras unless a local customer explicitly grants permission. Flock says it has implemented safeguards since 2024, including removing federal agencies from statewide and national lookup networks in August 2025, restricting federal agencies to one-to-one sharing only, and deploying automatic keyword blocks for immigration-related searches, adding that federal pilot programs have concluded. (Vendor position.)

articles.title: Denver extends contract for Flock cameras with new safeguards against sharing with immigration enforcement
articles.content: Denver will extend its Flock contract with new privacy protections. The program uses cameras at 70 intersections to capture plates, aiding crime-solving and auto-theft reduction. Under a five-month no-cost extension through March 31, 2026, data is restricted to Denver PD and Colorado agencies with MOUs; federal agents cannot access it. Unauthorized sharing with immigration enforcement triggers $100,000 fines and contract termination, and Flock agreed to pay $100,000 for data breaches. Since 2024 the program contributed to 352 arrests, 39 firearm recoveries, and over 250 stolen-vehicle recoveries. Long-term approval depends on meeting conditions.
articles.author: Christa Swanson

articles.title: Cambridge stops using license plate reader cameras over data sharing concerns
articles.content: Cambridge's city council suspended Flock ALPR cameras after concerns about potential federal data sharing. Approved in February as a crime-solving tool, the decision reversed course after advocates raised privacy questions. Vice Mayor Marc McGovern said the council thought it had adequate protections but found them less solid than believed, and expressed concern about targeting innocent people without warrants. Governor Maura Healey supported responsible use of surveillance technology, noting cameras help solve and deter crime. Flock denied the allegations, saying questions about federal relationships have been addressed and prompted product improvements. The city is seeking alternatives.
articles.author: Logan Hall

articles.title: Leaving the Door Wide Open: Flock Surveillance Systems Expose Washington Data to Immigration Enforcement
articles.media_outlet: UW Center for Human Rights (Jackson School, University of Washington)
articles.content: UW researchers obtained public records from 31 Washington law enforcement agencies using Flock. They found three forms of immigration-enforcement access: 'front door' sharing enabled by eight agencies directly with U.S. Border Patrol; 'back door' access where Border Patrol searched at least ten agencies' networks without explicit authorization; and 'side door' searches where local officers ran Flock queries on behalf of federal immigration agents. The findings raise compliance concerns with Washington's Keep Washington Working law, which prohibits dedicating local resources to civil immigration enforcement, and broader privacy implications for residents.
articles.author: Andrea Marcos

articles.title: Flock Gives Law Enforcement All Over the Country Access to Your Location
articles.media_outlet: The Data for Justice Project, ACLU of Massachusetts
articles.content: As of July 2025, Flock operated nearly 7,000 networks and nearly 90,000 cameras nationwide. Over 80 Massachusetts police departments contracted with the company, spending more than $2 million over three years. The system uses reciprocal access: departments sharing data nationally gain access to search the entire nationwide database ('you show me yours, I'll show you mine'), enabled by clicking 'Enable National Lookup.' A single 30-day period in spring 2025 documented over 450,000 nationwide searches, often with vague justifications like 'investigation' or 'susp.' Officers in states such as Florida, Texas, Ohio could track Massachusetts residents; one case involved a Texas officer searching for a woman regarding an abortion investigation. Federal agencies including ICE and CBP have accessed the database.
articles.author: Gideon Epstein

articles.title: Flock's Gunshot Detection Microphones Will Start Listening for Human Voices
articles.content: Flock is expanding its acoustic gunshot-detection device 'Raven' to include 'human distress' detection, enabling deployed microphones to identify sounds like screaming and alert police. EFF raises concerns that the devices act as high-powered microphones in public spaces, with unclear functionality, potential conflicts with state eavesdropping laws, and historical accuracy problems (gunshot detectors often misidentify fireworks or backfires, leading to dangerous police responses). The article cites Flock's troubled record: violations of Illinois law regarding immigration-enforcement data access, a North Carolina licensing halt, and reinstalling cameras after removal in Evanston, Illinois. EFF urges cities to reconsider Flock contracts.
articles.author: Matthew Guariglia

articles.title: Anti-Surveillance Mapmaker Refuses Flock Safety's Cease-and-Desist Demand
articles.content: Privacy activist Will Freeman created DeFlock.me, mapping over 16,000 ALPR camera locations across the U.S., more than one-third of them Flock devices. When Flock sent a cease-and-desist letter claiming trademark dilution, EFF defended the project as protected First Amendment speech and commentary, noting federal anti-dilution law exempts noncommercial use and criticism. The letter highlighted that ALPRs enable mass surveillance by tracking vehicles and creating detailed 'fingerprints' (make, model, color) regardless of criminal connection. EFF characterized the action as a 'trademark bully' tactic to intimidate under-resourced activists.
articles.author: Dave Maass; Cara Gagliano

articles.title: Vehicle Fingerprinting Through Pervasive Camera Surveillance Likely Violates Fourth Amendment, Court Finds
articles.content: A federal court ruled that Norfolk's use of Flock ALPRs likely violates the Fourth Amendment. The system's hundreds of cameras create searchable databases tracking vehicle movements without warrants. The court found the surveillance 'notably similar' to Carpenter v. United States (2018), where the Supreme Court recognized a reasonable expectation of privacy in long-term movement records. The decision rejected the city's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged Fourth Amendment violations and had standing. The ruling suggests querying location databases without warrants can constitute unconstitutional searches.

articles.title: Lawsuit: license plate readers found in CT violate 4th Amendment
articles.content: The Institute for Justice filed a federal lawsuit against Norfolk, Virginia challenging Flock's ALPR system as unconstitutional; similar cameras are installed in Connecticut towns (Cheshire, Darien, New Canaan, Southington). Cameras capture and store vehicle data for 30 days without warrant requirements. Plaintiffs argue officers can access the database without probable cause, tracking movements regardless of suspicion, violating the Fourth Amendment, and that Flock maintains a centralized database accessible across 5,000+ communities. Connecticut data showed limited results: Cheshire's 12 cameras identified 276,583 vehicles in 30 days, with only 495 flagged through crime databases.
articles.author: Katherine Revello

articles.title: Aerodome, Flock Safety partner to expand Drone as First Responder technology for public safety
articles.content: Aerodome and Flock Safety announced a partnership integrating drone-as-first-responder technology with Flock's platform. When Flock's plate recognition or audio sensors identify incidents (AMBER-alert vehicles, gunshots), automated triggers dispatch Aerodome drones within seconds. Scottsdale, Arizona is the initial deployment city. Police Chief Jeff Walther said the integration empowers first responders, reduces response times, and helps drive down crime by combining aerial intelligence with Flock's video, audio, and license plate recognition network for real-time situational awareness.
articles.author: Police1 Staff

articles.title: What are ALPRs? (DeFlock — Learn)
articles.content:
What are ALPRs?

Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs or LPRs) are AI-powered cameras that capture and analyze images of all passing vehicles, storing details like your car's location, date, and time. They also capture your car's make, model, color, and identifying features such as dents, roof racks, and bumper stickers, often turning these into searchable data points.

These cameras collect data on millions of vehicles regardless of whether the driver is suspected of a crime. These systems are marketed as indispensable tools to fight crime, but they ignore the powerful tools police already have to track criminals, such as cell phone location data, creating a loophole that doesn't require a warrant.

For a detailed explanation of how ALPRs are a threat to privacy, DeFlock points to an ACLU article as well as an EFF article on ALPRs.

== WHY YOU SHOULD BE CONCERNED ==

ALPRs Do Not Reduce Crime
There's no independent research proving that ALPRs can reduce crime. Headlines and supporting studies claiming otherwise are often produced by the companies selling ALPRs and the police agencies buying them.

For example, Flock Safety claims that 10% of reported crime in the U.S. is solved using Flock technology. The study that Flock cites was conducted by two Flock employees and “given legitimacy with the 'oversight' of two academic researchers whose names are also on the paper” according to a report by 404 Media. Flock Safety is using the veneer of an academic study as part of its sales pitch.

What research does exist regarding the ability of ALPRs to reduce crime is inconclusive at best:

“Our findings indicate that, when small numbers of LPR patrols are used in crime hot spots in the way we have tested them here, they do not seem to generate either a general or offense-specific deterrent effect.” — Journal of Experimental Criminology

“There is not even a moderate degree of correlation between ALPRs and stolen vehicle recoveries, let alone any apparent causality.” — Automated License Plate Readers: A Study in Failure

ALPRs Are a Major Security Risk
Companies that make ALPRs have a history of poor security practices, which can lead to data breaches and unauthorized access to sensitive information. For example:

• In November 2025, a security researcher found Flock logins for sale on Russian hacking forums, since Flock negligently doesn't require multifactor authentication, an alleged violation of federal law and industry standard security practices.
• In January 2025, Motorola Solutions' ALPR system was found to have a critical security flaw that allowed anyone to access live data from their cameras. Data includes license plate numbers, make, model, color, and timestamps. A live feed of both cameras (color and infrared) was also available to stream using a web browser.
• In July 2025, Flock Safety exposed a misconfigured demo site that included (1) their internal search interface and some source code, some of which reveals how they calculate confidence scores for vehicle tracking and (2) a live ArcGIS admin API key, which included access to over 50 private data layers.

ALPRs Are Dragnet Surveillance
A study of ALPRs in Piedmont, CA, found that less than 0.3% of ALPR hits might translate into a useful investigative lead. Most license plates recorded were not on a hot list, yet police still logged information on people's movements throughout the day.

Flock Safety provides Transparency Portals to their police customers, which allow the public to see the data collected by ALPRs. From these portals, we can see that the vast majority of license plates scanned are not on a hot list (vehicles suspected of being involved in crimes), e.g., the Oak Park, IL and Vallejo, CA Transparency Portals.

ALPRs Are Abused
There are many documented cases where police have knowingly used ALPRs to commit crimes and put people in danger. These examples illustrate that it can be difficult to put meaningful restrictions in place that prevent ALPRs from being used for nefarious purposes. It's often only after harm is done that an officer is caught and punished, if at all:

• Texas police used Flock ALPRs to track a woman who had an abortion across state lines.
• A police officer used Flock Safety ALPRs to stalk his estranged wife in Kechi, KS.
• A police officer accepted a bribe to run a woman's license plate in Georgia.
• A police officer used ALPRs to stalk his ex-girlfriend in Ohio.
• California agencies kept data longer than necessary and shared it with unauthorized agencies.
• Police in San Diego County broke the law sharing drivers' data.

ALPR Usage Leads to Dangerous Police Encounters
The negligent use of ALPRs has led to dangerous police encounters, including pulling guns on innocent drivers. Here are just a few examples:

• A San Francisco woman was pulled out of her car at gunpoint because of a license plate reader error.
• Police terrorized a Black family but blamed a license plate reader for misidentifying a 'stolen' vehicle.
• Deputies were sued after a false ALPR hit led to a guns-out traffic stop of a California privacy activist.
• A privacy advocate sued Contra Costa sheriff's deputies after license plate readers falsely targeted his car as stolen.
• A Denver woman had to prove her innocence after detectives relied on Flock cameras to pin a $25 package theft on her.

ALPRs Result in Racist Policing
ALPRs are more likely to surveil communities with a higher density of Black and brown people, reinforcing systemic racism in policing.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation reviewed the use of ALPRs by the Oakland Police Department and found that ALPR cameras were more likely to scan license plates in communities with a higher density of Black and brown people than in communities with a higher density of white people.

A report by The Associated Press shows that after 9/11, the NYPD used ALPRs to monitor Muslims visiting mosques.

A study of Flock Safety's impact in Oak Park, IL found: “In the first 10 months of their use, 84% of the drivers stopped by Oak Park police because of Flock were Black.” — Freedom to Thrive Oak Park

ALPRs Put Undocumented People at Risk
Police agencies frequently share ALPR data with ICE, putting undocumented people at risk, even in states where this is legally prohibited:

• ICE taps into Flock's nationwide camera network, data shows.

== FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS ==

Q: Are ALPRs a necessary tool for police?
A: No. Police have always had methods to obtain location information for suspects of crimes. These methods used to require establishing probable cause and obtaining a search warrant, which provides oversight and accountability as required by the 4th Amendment. ALPRs, on the other hand, collect location data on all of us, and they are searched without any warrants or oversight.

Q: Why should I care if I have nothing to hide?
A: 1. You don't get to decide what looks suspicious tomorrow. Just because you're not doing anything wrong today doesn't mean you won't be watched tomorrow. License plate cameras like Flock don't know your intentions—only your movements. A trip to a protest, a friend's house in a “high-crime” area, or even a misread plate can flag you as “suspicious.” As history has shown, when governments or third parties gain unchecked surveillance powers, they're eventually used against people who weren't doing anything wrong—until someone decided they were. For example, until early in 2025, ALPRs weren't used for tracking immigrants, legal or otherwise, but now they are, despite policies prohibiting it.

2. Mistakes happen, and you're the one who pays for them. Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) are not always accurate. People have been pulled over at gunpoint, arrested, or detained because a camera misread a plate or flagged the wrong car. If you “have nothing to hide,” you also have nothing to correct the record with when a machine error points the finger at you.

Q: Do these cameras only record vehicles involved in crimes?
A: No, ALPRs record all vehicles that pass by, not just those involved in crimes. They capture license plates, unique identifying features, locations, dates, and times of every vehicle, regardless of whether the driver is suspected of wrongdoing. This means that even if you're not doing anything wrong, your movements are still being tracked and stored, often for long periods of time.

Additionally, the data collected by ALPRs can be shared with other law enforcement agencies and third parties, further extending the reach of this surveillance. This raises significant privacy concerns, as most individuals are not aware that their movements are being monitored and recorded.

Q: Do police need a warrant to search these cameras?
A: No, police do not need a warrant to search these cameras. The data collected by ALPRs is owned by the police department, and law enforcement agencies can access it without a warrant. There is often no oversight at all on how these searches are conducted, raising concerns about their constitutionality under the Fourth Amendment.

Some agencies have implemented agency-wide ALPR policies, but these policies are meaningless, as most agencies have opted into an extensive data sharing network that allows other agencies to access their data without the same restrictions, with tens of thousands of national searches occurring on a daily basis.

Q: What oversight is there for these systems?
A: There is little to no oversight for these systems. While some police departments have implemented policies regarding the use of ALPRs, these policies are often weak and poorly enforced. Many agencies do not have any policies at all, and there is no requirement for transparency or accountability in how these systems are used.

While Flock offers a transparency portal for their law enforcement customers, they allow their customers to cherry-pick what information is included or excluded from the portal. They also lack any meaningful data, often underreporting the number of agencies with access. Many activists believe the hotlist hits section is inflated to make it appear that the cameras are more effective than they actually are.

Q: Do Flock's transparency portals give a full picture of who has access to the data?
A: Absolutely not. Flock's transparency portals are notoriously incomplete and often misleading. They allow law enforcement agencies to cherry-pick what information is included or excluded, leading to significant underreporting of the number of organizations with access to the data.

Take Boulder, Colorado for example. Their transparency portal lists around 90 agencies with access to their ALPR data. However, a public records request revealed that over 6,000 agencies actually had access. This discrepancy highlights the lack of transparency and accountability in Flock's reporting.

Q: Can Flock be trusted to keep our data safe?
A: Absolutely not. In November 2025, a security researcher found Flock logins for sale on Russian hacking forums, since Flock negligently doesn't require multifactor authentication, an alleged violation of federal law and industry standard security practices.

Flock has also been caught several times lying on the record. For example, their CEO was interviewed by Denver 9News, and he claimed that Flock had no federal contracts. However, a couple weeks later, 9News discovered that Border Patrol actually did have access to search Flock's systems. Flock described the data sharing agreement as “one-to-one”, meaning an agency would have to accept the data sharing request from Border Patrol.

Doubtful of this claim, DeFlock filed a public records request with the Boulder Police Department in Colorado, and found that “U.S. Border Patrol” was searching over 6,000 agencies, consistent with the number of agencies on the national network at the time. Either every agency on the national network happily accepted Border Patrol's request to their data, or Flock was lying on the record yet again.

Q: How can I get these cameras out of my city/town?
A: Several cities in the US have killed contracts for ALPRs, such as Denver and Austin. An effective strategy is to raise concerns in your community, build a group of advocates, and petition the city council not to extend the contract.
